name: Aarav
text:
Design thinking has five stages.

1. Empathize - understanding the users and their feelings.
2. Define - defining the problem clearly.
3. Ideate - generating ideas through brainstorming.
4. Prototype - making a model of the solution.
5. Test - testing the prototype with users.

Problem: The canteen needs a mobile app for ordering food.

Solution: We can make an app so students can order food.

[Diagram of 5 stages drawn]

Conclusion: Design thinking is a user-centred approach used to solve problems.

name: Aarav
text:
Scenario: LICET canteen, 12:30-1:10 lunch break. Users: students with a class at 1:10, and canteen counter staff.

Diagram: [Five stages drawn as a loop: Empathize -> Define -> Ideate -> Prototype -> Test, with arrows from Test back to Define and Ideate labelled 'iterate']

1. Empathize
Observed the queue on 3 days at 12:30 (about 60 students, average wait 14 min) and interviewed 6 students and 2 staff.
Empathy map: [Says: 'I don't have time to eat'; Thinks: 'Will I be marked late?'; Does: sends one friend to order for four, skips lunch; Feels: rushed, anxious]
Insight: the problem is unpredictability - students don't know if they will make it back in time.

2. Define (POV)
A student with a 40-minute lunch break needs to get food quickly and predictably because arriving late to class costs attendance.
HMW: How might we make lunch wait time predictable? How might we spread the 12:30 rush?

3. Ideate
Diverge: (a) pre-order with pickup time slots, (b) express counter for snacks, (c) live queue display at the block entrance, (d) staggered lunch timings per department, (e) pre-packed combo meals.
Converge using an impact/feasibility matrix: (a) and (b) are high impact and feasible this semester; (d) needs admin approval. Chosen: pre-order with 10-minute pickup slots plus an express snacks counter.

4. Prototype
Low-fidelity paper prototype of the red route: menu -> pick combo -> choose pickup slot -> pay via UPI -> pickup token screen.

5. Test
5 students; task: 'order lunch for a 12:40 pickup'. Measure time to order (target under 1 min) and queue time at pickup (target under 3 min). Two testers could not find the slot picker -> iterate: move slot choice before payment and make it the primary button.

Result: predictable pickup reduces late arrivals; next iteration tests slot capacity with the canteen staff.

name: Priya
text:
Users: students in the lunch queue and canteen staff.

Empathize: I watched the queue at lunch and spoke to 5 students. They said they wait 15 minutes and often skip lunch.
Empathy map: [Says 'no time'; Thinks 'I'll be late'; Does skips lunch; Feels stressed]

Define: Students need to get lunch within their short break because otherwise they are late for class.

Ideate: Build a mobile app where students can order and pay before lunch.

Prototype: Make the app in Figma.

Test: Show it to students.

[Diagram: Empathize -> Define -> Ideate -> Prototype -> Test]

name: Rahul
text:
Scenario: long canteen queues at lunch; students late for class.

[Diagram: five boxes in a straight line, Empathize to Test]

Empathize: Observe the queue, interview students and staff. Students are stressed about attendance.

Define: The canteen should have a pre-ordering system.

Ideate: Ideas - pre-order app, more counters, token system, snack counter. Choose the pre-order app because it is the most modern.

Prototype: Wireframes of menu, cart and payment screens.

Test: 5 students try to order lunch; measure how long it takes and fix problems they face.

name: Meera
text:
Scenario and users: LICET canteen during the 40-minute lunch break. Primary users: students with a post-lunch class; secondary: counter staff handling the rush.

Diagram: [Design thinking loop - Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test in a circle, arrows from Test back to Define and Ideate; each stage annotated with the canteen activity below]

Empathize: Contextual observation 12:25-12:55 for three days (counted queue length every 5 min: peak 55 people at 12:35) and 8 short interviews.
Empathy map - Says: 'I just grab chips now'; Thinks: 'If I'm late again my attendance drops'; Does: orders for friends, eats while walking; Feels: anxious, hungry. Pain: unpredictable wait. Gain: knowing exactly when food is ready.

Define: POV - A student with a fixed 40-minute break needs a predictable lunch wait because being late to the next class affects attendance.
HMW reduce uncertainty about wait time? HMW reduce the 12:35 peak?

Ideate (diverge): pre-order with pickup slots; express snacks counter; live queue-time display; staggered breaks; combo pre-packs; SMS when order ready.
Converge (dot voting + impact/effort 2x2): pre-order with slots (high impact, medium effort) and live queue display (medium impact, low effort). Staggered breaks rejected - outside our control.

Prototype: Paper prototype of the red route (menu -> combo -> pickup slot -> UPI -> token), plus a sketch of the queue display.

Test: 5 students, think-aloud, task 'order for 12:40 pickup'. Metrics: task success, time on task, wait at pickup. Finding: slot picker missed by 2 of 5 -> moved before payment. Next iteration: test slot capacity limits with staff.

name: Aarav
text:
Heuristic evaluation of the college fee-payment page using Nielsen's heuristics.

1. Visibility of system status: after clicking 'Pay', the page shows no progress indicator, so students click twice and are charged twice. Fix: show a spinner and disable the button.
2. Match between system and real world: the page says 'Remit dues' instead of 'Pay fees'. Fix: use the words students use.
3. Error prevention: the amount field accepts any value. Fix: pre-fill the due amount and lock it.
4. Recognition rather than recall: students must remember their 12-digit register number. Fix: auto-fill it after login.
5. Help users recognise and recover from errors: a failed payment shows 'Error 502'. Fix: say whether money was deducted and what to do next.

[Annotated screenshot of the fee page with the five problems marked]

Conclusion: fixing these five issues would reduce double payments and help-desk calls.
